title: A monthly check-in
tomorrow: Ông booked a temple retreat for when Mai's home. is she ready?

cards: Nearly two weeks in, Mai's mom calls on her lunch break at the pharmacy. Between questions about food and sleep, she asks one that lands: are you still you? Mai laughs, then can't answer.
How would anyone check? The Buddha gave his own son a tool for exactly that, and there's one hanging in your bathroom: a mirror.

teach.b: In the Majjhima Nikaya, the Buddha asks young Rahula: what is a mirror for? For reflecting, Rahula says. So too with what you do, the Buddha tells him.
Before an act, while doing it, and after it's done, look: does this lead to harm, for me, for others, or both? If you see harm, own it to a wise friend and hold back next time.
If you see none, stay with the gladness and keep training. That's the teaching under a monthly check-in. Not a mood score, and not a verdict.
A mirror, held up at intervals, to see what your actions actually did.

The Dhammapada gives the pace in Max Müller's words: "Let a wise man blow off the impurities of his self, as a smith blows off the impurities of silver, one by one, little by little, and from time to time."
From time to time. Month by month. A neighbor tradition keeps a close cousin of this.
The Psalms, prayed by Jews and Christians, ask in the King James words: "So teach us to number our days, that we may apply our hearts unto wisdom."
What's shared is real: stopping to count your time so it turns into wisdom. The difference is honest too.
The psalm is a prayer, asking God to teach. The mirror is a tool the Buddha hands you for looking at your own acts and what follows from them. Two ways of counting days.

how: Buddhists reflect on their actions in different rhythms: daily reflection, the monks' fortnightly confession on uposatha days, and personal reviews; some practitioners set a monthly time to look back over their practice and conduct.

o: grading yourself on a scale every thirty days
looking back each month at what your actions did
a monthly appointment with a teacher or monk

games.q: mirrors and smiths — tap the pairs.
p: the Buddha's son, shown a mirror

s: the Buddha's mirror teaching is about judging yourself harshly
if you see harm, own it and hold back next time; if you see none, stay with the gladness and keep training.
the Buddha taught his son Rahula with a question about a mirror
what is a mirror for? for reflecting. so too with every act.
the psalm's 'number our days' and the Buddha's mirror are the same practice
both stop to look at time and life; the psalm asks God to teach, the mirror looks at one's own acts.

games.q: your sister writes resolutions every January and never looks at them again until the next one. what does today's teaching add?
o: look in the mirror more often: a short check each month, little by little
make the list longer, so there's more to work on all year
drop the list; checking on yourself is just self-criticism
games.why: the smith clears silver 'one by one, little by little, and from time to time.' a monthly mirror keeps the work small and steady.

practice: Write one question by hand that you'll ask yourself at the end of every month, a mirror question about what your actions did, to you and to others. Keep it short enough to remember.
Then sit with it for two minutes without answering yet.

wordCard.voice: A monthly check-in: a mirror held up at the month's end, to see what your actions did.

orig.note: Pali: reviewing, looking back over. The word the mirror teaching turns on.

carryVoice: Here it is: month by month, the mirror and the smith, a little at a time. Good night.

sources.q: Let a wise man blow off the impurities of his self, as a smith blows off the impurities of silver, one by one, little by little, and from time to time.
So teach us to number our days, that we may apply our hearts unto wisdom.
